segments.text: A good company at the wrong price is a bad investment. Remember this line.

Are the numbers real? So secondly, we check three years' financial statements of the company, and these financial statements you will find from the Red Herring Prospectus itself. We check whether the revenues are consistent. Is the company making profits, or are these numbers which are only promising in nature? So the most important thing is: check cash flow from the operations. Profit is an opinion, but cash is a reality. Cash is a fact. Company doing profit with negative operating cash flow is a red flag. And also check the debt. If IPO money is going to repay loans, find out why the company borrowed so much in the first place.

The RHP has a section called Basis for Offer Price. It compares the company's P/E ratio with listed peers. Say the industry trades at 30 times earnings, and this IPO is priced at 60 times. You are paying double, so the company must grow much faster just to justify the price. Many IPOs are priced for perfection, because the seller wants the maximum price. And remember, the seller knows the business far better than you. So the full checklist is available on the channel.
